intro: A compact 120V dryer plugs into an ordinary outlet and fits where a full-size machine never could. Here are five worth buying, plus the venting, circuit and lint rules that keep one safe in an apartment.

A portable dryer is a trade: you give up capacity and speed in exchange for a machine that runs on a standard 120V outlet and fits in a closet. That trade is worth making in plenty of apartments, but only if you respect two things a small dryer still shares with a big one. The hot, wet, lint-filled air has to go somewhere safe, and the heater draws enough current to deserve its own circuit.

sections.h: What Actually Matters in a Portable Dryer

blocks.p: Start with the electrical supply, because it decides which dryers are even on the table. A standard full-size electric dryer runs on 240V and needs a dedicated 30A circuit and a large receptacle. A portable or compact 120V dryer plugs into an ordinary household outlet. If your apartment has no dryer hookup, a 120V machine is usually the only electric dryer you can use without an electrician, which is why this guide focuses on them.

Next is venting. A conventional dryer heats air, blows it through the clothes and pushes it out of the machine carrying water vapor and lint. That exhaust has to go outdoors through a proper duct or window vent, or the machine has to be a genuine ventless design that condenses the moisture inside. Where the exhaust goes is the single biggest practical question for anyone putting a dryer in an apartment, and it is covered in detail below.

Then capacity. Compact dryers run from small tabletop units of around 1.5 cu ft to roughly 3.5 to 4 cu ft for the larger compact models. A full-size dryer is typically well over 7 cu ft. The dryer drum should be roughly twice the size of the washer drum it pairs with, because clothes need room to tumble. A 2.6 cu ft dryer pairs well with a 1.6 cu ft portable washer; a tiny 1.5 cu ft unit is for very small loads.

Finally, speed. A 120V heater is much smaller than a 240V heater, so a compact dryer takes longer to dry the same weight of clothes. That is not a defect; it is physics. How wet the clothes are going in matters a lot, which is why the spin speed of your washer and a separate spin dryer can cut drying time more than any setting on the dryer itself.

If you are still choosing the washer, plan the pair together. Our [guide to portable washers](/best-portable-washer/) covers the sink-connected machines that pair with these dryers, including twin tubs whose separate spinners leave clothes drier going in.

sections.h: 120V vs 240V: Why a Compact Dryer Is Slower

blocks.p: The difference between a 120V and a 240V dryer is mostly about how much heat the machine can make. Power is voltage times current. A 240V dryer on a 30A circuit can run a heating element several times larger than anything that can safely run on a 120V household circuit. More heat means more water evaporated per minute, which is why a full-size electric dryer finishes a big load in under an hour while a compact 120V model takes longer on a much smaller one.

A 120V compact dryer is limited by the outlet. A typical 15A or 20A household circuit can only supply so much power, and a dryer runs for long stretches, so its heater has to be sized well under the circuit's limit. The result is a machine that dries gently and slowly. For many people that is fine, especially for a single person running a load in the evening, but it is worth knowing before you expect full-size performance.

Some larger compact dryers are built for 240V, often with a choice of 120V or 240V depending on the model. They dry faster, but they need a 240V receptacle and circuit, usually the same 30A dryer circuit a full-size machine would use. If your apartment already has a dryer hookup, a compact 240V model or even a stackable full-depth pair may be a better choice than a portable one. Our [dryer cord guide](/best-dryer-cord/) covers the three- and four-prong cords and receptacles those machines use.

Do not try to adapt between the two. A 240V dryer cannot be safely plugged into a 120V outlet with an adapter, and a 120V dryer should never be wired onto a 240V circuit. Buy the dryer that matches the receptacle you have, or have a licensed electrician install the receptacle you need, with a permit where your jurisdiction requires one.
THE RULE
Match the dryer to the outlet you have.

No dryer hookup: buy a 120V compact and plan on a dedicated circuit. An existing 240V dryer receptacle: consider a 240V compact or full-size machine instead, because it will dry much faster. Never adapt one to the other.

blocks.p: What the table cannot show is drying time, because it depends far more on how wet the clothes are going in than on the dryer. A load spun hard in a fast washer dries much sooner in a compact dryer than the same load out of a small portable washer with a gentle spin. That is why the spin dryer earns a place on this list despite not heating anything.

Controls vary from a simple timer knob to electronic panels with sensor drying. Sensor drying, where the machine stops when the clothes are dry, saves energy and reduces over-drying, but the main thing a compact dryer needs is a clear lint filter that is easy to reach and clean. Check where the filter sits before you buy, because one that is fiddly to remove is one you will be tempted to skip.

If you are tempted by an all-in-one washer-dryer combo, treat it as a separate category. Combos save space but are usually larger, heavier, more expensive and slower per load than a separate washer and dryer. They make sense where you can only fit one machine. For a renter who moves every couple of years, a separate portable washer and compact dryer is usually the more flexible choice.

sections.h: Venting, Vent Kits and Ventless Designs

blocks.p: A conventional dryer, including most compact 120V models, is a vented dryer. It pushes hot, moist, lint-laden air out of an exhaust port, and that air has to go outdoors. Residential codes generally require dryer exhaust to terminate outside the building, and dryer manuals specify the duct type and maximum length. Venting a standard dryer into a closet or living room dumps moisture and fine lint into the space, which feeds mold, damages drywall and leaves lint on every surface.

For apartments without a wall vent, the usual answer is a window vent kit: a panel that fits in the window opening with a duct port, connected to the dryer by a short duct. Keep the run as short and straight as possible, use rigid or semi-rigid metal duct rather than plastic or thin foil, and make sure the outside end has a flap that closes when the dryer is off. Long, kinked or crushed ducts trap lint and slow drying, and both raise the fire risk.

Some compact dryer manuals describe an indoor exhaust option, such as a lint bag or filter box on the exhaust port. Only use it if your specific manual permits it, and understand what it does and does not do. It catches some lint, but all of the water still goes into the room. A load of wet clothes holds a surprising amount of water, and in a small apartment that humidity condenses on windows and walls. If you go this route, run a dehumidifier; our [dehumidifier guide](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) covers models that can keep up.

A true ventless dryer is a different design. Condenser dryers cool the exhaust air inside the machine and collect the water in a tank or send it to a drain; heat pump dryers do the same more efficiently. They are built to run without an outdoor vent, but they still release some heat, need their lint filters and condenser cleaned and usually cost more. Most ventless models are full-size or 24-inch compact units, many on 240V. A vented dryer with an indoor lint bag is not a ventless dryer.

Never vent any dryer into a wall cavity, attic, crawl space or ceiling, and never connect it to a bathroom fan duct. All of these trap lint and moisture where you cannot see or clean them. If you cannot vent outdoors and your manual does not permit indoor use, either choose a genuine ventless design or air-dry on a rack. That is not the answer people want, but it is the safe one.

sections.h: Outlets, Dedicated Circuits and Extension Cords

blocks.p: A 120V compact dryer is one of the largest loads you can plug into an ordinary outlet. Its heater runs for long stretches, which is exactly the kind of load that exposes weak connections and overloaded circuits. Check the nameplate or manual for the dryer's rated current and the circuit it requires. Many manuals call for a dedicated circuit, meaning nothing else is plugged into that circuit while the dryer runs.

A dedicated 20A circuit is the conservative choice for a heated compact dryer, and some manuals specify it. A 15A circuit shared with a microwave, a space heater or a hair dryer will trip, and repeated tripping is a sign the circuit is being pushed too hard. If you are not sure what else is on the circuit, our [circuit breaker finder guide](/best-circuit-breaker-finder/) covers the tools that map outlets to breakers in minutes.

Plug the dryer straight into a wall outlet. Do not use an extension cord, a power strip or a light-duty adapter. The plug and outlet should fit snugly; a loose, warm or discolored outlet is a warning sign, and you should stop using it and have it checked. Adding a new circuit or upgrading an outlet is a job for a licensed electrician, with a permit where required, and in a rental it is the landlord's decision and usually the landlord's cost.

Electronic controls on newer dryers are sensitive to voltage spikes from lightning and utility switching. A point-of-use surge protector rated for appliances helps, and a whole-house surge protector at the panel protects every appliance at once. Our [whole-house surge protector guide](/best-whole-house-surge-protector/) explains how those devices work and why they need an electrician to install them.

A heated dryer is not a good match for most portable power stations. Its heater draws a large continuous load that would drain a typical station quickly. A generator can run one, but only outdoors, far from doors and windows, because generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide. Never run a generator in a garage or indoors, and never plug one into a wall outlet to backfeed the house. During an outage, a spin dryer and a drying rack are the practical choice.

Compact dryers work best with modest loads. The drum needs empty space for clothes to tumble through the hot air; a packed drum dries slowly, unevenly and with more wrinkles. A good rule is to fill the drum about half to two-thirds full with wet clothes. If you are pairing it with a portable washer, one washer load per dryer load is usually about right, and splitting a big wash across two dryer runs often finishes sooner than one overloaded run.

Drying time depends mainly on how much water is in the clothes, the fabric and the heater size. Light synthetics dry quickly; cotton towels and jeans take longest. Manufacturers rarely publish meaningful drying times for compact dryers because the variables are so large. Owners commonly report that a mixed load from a small portable washer takes noticeably longer than an hour, while the same load spun harder dries faster. Use the times on your manual as a starting point, not a promise.

The cheapest way to speed up a compact dryer is to put drier clothes into it. Use the highest spin your washer offers, run an extra spin on heavy items, or use a separate spin dryer before the heated dryer. Removing water by spinning takes far less energy than evaporating it with heat, and it shortens the dryer's run time, which also reduces wear and the amount of lint in the exhaust.

Sort by weight. Drying towels and jeans with T-shirts means the light items finish long before the heavy ones, and the dryer keeps running to finish the towels while the shirts overheat. Separate loads of similar weight dry more evenly and faster. Clean the lint filter before every load, because a clogged filter restricts airflow and adds time to every cycle.

sections.h: Stacking Kits, Wall Mounts and Lint Fire Safety

blocks.p: Many compact front-load dryers can be stacked on top of a matching compact front-load washer with a stacking kit sold by the manufacturer, and some can be wall-mounted with a manufacturer kit. Use only the kit specified in the manual for your exact models, because the kit has to hold the dryer's weight and keep it from walking off the washer during spin. Never stack a dryer on top of a top-loading portable washer, which has a lid that needs to open and a cabinet not built to carry weight.

If you wall-mount a dryer, mount it into studs or solid blocking with the hardware the manufacturer specifies, at a height where you can reach the lint filter without strain. A dryer pulled off a wall by its own vibration is a serious hazard. If you are not confident in finding studs and choosing fasteners, hire someone who is. In a rental, ask before drilling.

Lint is the fire risk to take seriously. The NFPA identifies failure to clean the dryer as a leading cause of home dryer fires, and lint is highly flammable. Clean the lint filter before every load. Every few months, disconnect and clean the duct and the vent kit, and check the outdoor flap opens freely. If the dryer is suddenly taking longer, the outside of the machine feels hot, or you smell scorching, stop using it and check the duct.

Use the dryer when you are home and awake. Do not start a load and leave the apartment or go to sleep. Keep the area around the dryer clear of boxes, laundry baskets and cleaning products, and have a working smoke alarm nearby. Do not dry items stained with oil, gasoline, cooking oil or solvents, which can ignite even after washing; air-dry those instead.

Moisture is the other long-term issue. Even a properly vented dryer warms and humidifies the room through its cabinet and door seals. In a small, closed space, keep the door open or add ventilation. If you see condensation on windows or musty smells after laundry day, our [guide to air purifiers for mold](/best-air-purifier-for-mold/) and dehumidifier guides cover how to bring humidity back under control.

If you have a standard outlet on a circuit you can dedicate to the dryer and a window you can vent through, buy the Magic Chef MCSDRY15W. Its 2.6 cu ft drum is the right size to pair with a 1.6 cu ft portable washer, it runs on 120V, and Magic Chef's compact laundry line is widely sold and easy to find support for. It is the default pick for most apartments.

If you already own or want a BLACK+DECKER portable washer, the BLACK+DECKER BCED26 is the matching alternative at a similar size. If you wash bigger loads and have the electrical supply for it, look at the larger BCED37, but confirm the voltage and circuit requirement on the listing first. A larger drum is only worth it if your outlet and circuit can support the machine as specified.

If you are drying a few items at a time, live alone in a very small space or need the lowest price, a mini dryer like the COSTWAY Compact Laundry Dryer handles small loads of light clothing. Do not expect it to dry towels and jeans for two people. It still needs to be vented properly and plugged directly into the wall.

If you cannot vent a heated dryer, or you want to cut the time and cost of any dryer, buy the Laundry Alternative Nina Soft Spin Dryer. It uses no heat, so it adds no humidity beyond what drips into its drain, and it pulls a lot of water out of a load in a few minutes. Paired with a drying rack, it is a complete drying setup for many apartments, and paired with a heated compact dryer, it shortens every cycle.

Skip any compact dryer with a vague listing, no clear model number and no downloadable manual. You need the installation instructions to vent and power the machine correctly, and you need a real brand behind it for parts like belts and heating elements. Also skip the idea of venting a standard dryer into the room to save on a vent kit; the vent kit is cheaper than a mold problem.

mistakes: Venting a standard dryer into the room

A conventional dryer pushes hot, wet, lint-filled air out of its exhaust. Dumped into a closet or living space, that means mold, damp walls and lint everywhere. Vent outdoors with a short metal duct and window kit, use an indoor exhaust option only if your manual explicitly permits it, or choose a true ventless design.
Using an extension cord or shared circuit

A heated dryer is a long, heavy load that overheats light cords and power strips and trips shared circuits. Plug it directly into a wall outlet, check the nameplate current and keep the circuit free of other heavy loads. If the outlet is loose or warm, stop and have a licensed electrician look at it.

Lint is highly flammable, and failure to clean is a leading cause of home dryer fires. Clean the lint filter before every load, clean the duct and vent kit every few months, and treat longer drying times, a hot cabinet or a scorching smell as a reason to stop and check the duct immediately.

A packed drum dries slowly and unevenly and runs the heater longer than necessary. Fill the drum about half to two-thirds full, sort loads by weight and split a big wash across two runs. Two moderate loads often finish sooner than one stuffed load, with fewer wrinkles and less wear.
Buying a 240V dryer for a 120V outlet

Full-size and some compact dryers need a 240V receptacle on a dedicated 30A circuit, and no adapter makes them safe on a household outlet. Check the electrical requirement on the spec sheet before buying, and if you need a new receptacle, have a licensed electrician install it with any required permit.
bottomLine: The best portable dryer is the one your outlet, your circuit and your window can support. For most apartments that is a 120V compact around 2.6 cu ft, led by the Magic Chef MCSDRY15W, with the BLACK+DECKER BCED26 as the matching alternative and the BCED37 for bigger loads if its electrical requirement fits your home. If you cannot vent at all, the Nina Soft Spin Dryer and a rack are the safe answer, and the COSTWAY mini dryer covers very small loads on a budget. Whatever you buy, vent it outdoors, plug it straight into the wall on its own circuit, clean the lint filter every load and never run it while you are out or asleep.

faqs.q: What is the best portable dryer for an apartment?
faqs.a: For most apartments, a 120V compact dryer around 2.6 cu ft, such as the Magic Chef MCSDRY15W or BLACK+DECKER BCED26, is the best fit. It plugs into a standard outlet, pairs well with a 1.6 cu ft portable washer and fits in a closet. You will still need a way to vent it outdoors, usually a window vent kit, and ideally a dedicated circuit.

faqs.q: Can a 120V clothes dryer plug into a regular outlet?
faqs.a: Yes, that is the point of a 120V compact dryer. Plug it directly into a grounded wall outlet, never into an extension cord or power strip, and keep other heavy loads off that circuit while it runs. Many manuals call for a dedicated circuit, often 20A. Check the nameplate and manual, and have a licensed electrician add a circuit if needed.

faqs.q: Is it safe to use a portable dryer without a vent?
faqs.a: Not a standard vented dryer. Without a vent, the moisture and fine lint go into your living space, causing mold and damp walls. Use an indoor exhaust option only if your manual explicitly permits it, and run a dehumidifier if you do. A true ventless condenser or heat pump dryer is designed to run without a vent, or use a spin dryer and a rack.

faqs.q: How long does a portable dryer take to dry a load?
faqs.a: Longer than a full-size dryer, because a 120V heater is much smaller. Drying time depends mostly on how wet the clothes are, the fabric and the load size, so manufacturers rarely publish firm times. Owners commonly report that loads from small portable washers can take well over an hour. Spinning clothes harder before drying is the most effective way to shorten it.

A ventless dryer removes moisture from the exhaust inside the machine instead of blowing it outdoors. Condenser dryers cool the air and collect water in a tank or drain line; heat pump dryers do the same more efficiently. They are designed to run without an outdoor vent. A vented dryer with an indoor lint bag is not a ventless dryer, because the moisture still enters the room.

faqs.q: Can I stack a portable dryer on a portable washer?
faqs.a: Only with a matching front-load compact washer and the manufacturer's stacking kit for those exact models. Never stack a dryer on a top-loading portable washer, whose lid has to open and whose cabinet is not built to carry weight. Some compact dryers can be wall-mounted with a manufacturer kit, which must be fastened into studs or solid blocking.

faqs.q: Can I run a portable dryer on a generator or power station?
faqs.a: A heated dryer would drain most portable power stations quickly because its heater is a large continuous load. A generator can run one, but only outdoors, well away from doors and windows, because of carbon monoxide. Never run a generator indoors or in a garage, and never plug one into a wall outlet. In an outage, a spin dryer and rack are more practical.
